stem:
A 71-year-old retired builder attends A&E after passing black stools for two days, preceded by a fortnight of gnawing upper abdominal pain. His medication review shows he buys naproxen over the counter for back pain and takes it most days.

Which item in his history is the most important contributor to his presentation?

options.E: Chronic heel pain from plantar fasciitis

correct_answer: A. Regular non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug use
why_correct: Naproxen and other NSAIDs reduce gastroduodenal mucosal protection and are a leading cause of peptic ulceration in older adults. Epigastric pain followed by melaena points to a bleeding ulcer, and daily over-the-counter use makes the NSAID the key modifiable risk factor. It should be stopped and gastroprotection considered.
why_wrong: B. Allergic rhinitis has no link with peptic ulceration. C. Presbycusis is unrelated to upper GI bleeding. D. Cataract surgery does not predispose to ulcers. E. Plantar fasciitis matters only if treated with NSAIDs; the condition itself does not cause bleeding.
pearl: Ask specifically about over-the-counter painkillers: many patients do not regard bought ibuprofen or naproxen as medication.
thinking: Epigastric pain then melaena ↓ Suggests bleeding peptic ulcer ↓ Search history for ulcer risk factors ↓ Daily over-the-counter naproxen ↓ NSAID use is the key contributor
exam_trap: E, Chronic heel pain from plantar fasciitis — it tempts because it is a reason he might take painkillers, but the condition itself is harmless; the drug is the risk.
takeaway: Always take a full drug history, including bought NSAIDs, in anyone with upper GI bleeding.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman who never takes painkillers sees her GP with several months of epigastric pain that wakes her at night and eases with food. She does not smoke and drinks little alcohol. A stool antigen test is requested.

Which underlying cause is most likely to explain her symptoms?

options.C: Helicobacter pylori colonisation of the stomach
options.D: Borrelia infection after a tick bite

correct_answer: C. Helicobacter pylori colonisation of the stomach
why_correct: Nocturnal epigastric pain relieved by eating suggests a duodenal ulcer, and in someone not using NSAIDs the commonest cause is Helicobacter pylori infection. The organism damages the mucosa and increases acid secretion. Stool antigen or urea breath testing confirms it, and eradication therapy heals the ulcer and prevents recurrence.
why_wrong: A. Campylobacter causes acute diarrhoeal illness, not chronic ulcer pain. B. Herpes zoster causes a painful dermatomal rash. D. Lyme disease causes erythema migrans and later neurological or joint features. E. Measles is an acute febrile illness with rash.
pearl: Stop proton pump inhibitors for two weeks before a urea breath test or stool antigen test, or a false-negative result may occur.
thinking: Chronic epigastric pain at night ↓ Eased by eating suggests duodenal ulcer ↓ No NSAID use ↓ Commonest remaining cause is H. pylori ↓ Confirm with stool antigen and eradicate
exam_trap: A, Campylobacter gut infection — another curved Gram-negative organism of the gut, but it causes acute gastroenteritis rather than peptic ulceration.
takeaway: In ulcer disease without NSAID use, think Helicobacter pylori first.

stem:
A 66-year-old man taking diclofenac for gout flares is found on endoscopy to have a gastric ulcer. He asks why his tablets damaged his stomach.

Which mechanism most directly accounts for this effect?

options.B: Overproduction of bile by the liver
options.D: Greater bicarbonate output from the pancreas
options.E: Reduced formation of protective prostaglandins through cyclo-oxygenase blockade

correct_answer: E. Reduced formation of protective prostaglandins through cyclo-oxygenase blockade
why_correct: NSAIDs block cyclo-oxygenase, particularly COX-1, which reduces prostaglandin synthesis in the gastric mucosa. These prostaglandins maintain mucus and bicarbonate secretion and mucosal blood flow, so their loss leaves the lining vulnerable to acid. A direct topical irritant effect adds to the damage.
why_wrong: A. Faster gastric emptying would, if anything, reduce acid contact time. B. Bile production is not the mechanism of NSAID injury. C. Insulin release is unrelated to ulcer formation. D. More pancreatic bicarbonate would neutralise duodenal acid rather than cause ulcers.
pearl: Proton pump inhibitor co-prescription is advised for people at higher risk of GI harm who need to continue an NSAID, such as older adults or those with previous ulcers.
thinking: Ulcer in a patient on diclofenac ↓ NSAIDs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase ↓ Fewer mucosal prostaglandins ↓ Less mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow ↓ Mucosa injured by acid
exam_trap: D, Greater bicarbonate output from the pancreas — bicarbonate sounds relevant to ulcers, but more bicarbonate would protect, and the key loss is in gastric mucosal defence.
takeaway: NSAIDs cause ulcers mainly by blocking prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection.

stem:
A 41-year-old delivery driver tells his GP that for several weeks he has had a gnawing ache high in the middle of his abdomen, typically a few hours after meals and in the early morning, which settles when he eats a snack. He takes ibuprofen regularly for migraine. Examination shows mild epigastric tenderness only.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Epigastric pain occurring when the stomach is empty and relieved by food is characteristic of a duodenal ulcer, because food buffers acid entering the duodenum. Regular ibuprofen use is a recognised risk factor, alongside Helicobacter pylori infection. The weeks-long, recurrent pattern with simple epigastric tenderness fits.
why_wrong: A. A ureteric stone causes severe colicky loin-to-groin pain. B. Gallbladder colic is usually triggered, not relieved, by eating, especially fatty food. C. Crohn's disease usually causes diarrhoea, weight loss and right iliac fossa pain. E. Appendicitis is an acute, progressive illness over hours to days.
pearl: Pain worse with eating suggests gastric ulcer and pain relieved by eating suggests duodenal ulcer, although the distinction is unreliable in practice.
thinking: Recurrent epigastric ache ↓ Occurs on an empty stomach ↓ Relieved by food ↓ Regular NSAID use ↓ Duodenal ulcer most likely
exam_trap: B, Gallbladder colic — it also causes epigastric pain related to meals, but it is provoked by eating rather than eased by it.
takeaway: Epigastric pain relieved by food in an NSAID user points to a duodenal ulcer.

stem:
A 61-year-old man is referred by his GP after several months of episodic purple-red facial flushing and watery diarrhoea; on two occasions he has also become wheezy. Abdominal imaging shows multiple liver deposits, and urinary 5-HIAA is raised.

Where is the primary tumour most likely to be?
correct_answer: D. Small intestine, typically the ileum
why_correct: Flushing, diarrhoea and bronchospasm with raised 5-HIAA indicate carcinoid syndrome. The commonest source is a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour of the small bowel, usually the ileum. Serotonin and other amines from gut tumours are normally inactivated by the liver, so the syndrome usually appears once liver metastases release mediators directly into the systemic circulation.
why_wrong: A. An adrenal medullary tumour (phaeochromocytoma) causes paroxysmal hypertension, headache and sweating. B. Hepatocellular carcinoma is a primary liver tumour and does not produce carcinoid syndrome; the liver lesions here are metastases. C. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma causes weight loss, pain and painless jaundice. E. Sigmoid adenocarcinoma presents with change in bowel habit and rectal bleeding.
pearl: Right-sided heart valve disease (tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis) is a late feature of carcinoid syndrome.
thinking: Flushing, diarrhoea and wheeze ↓ Raised urinary 5-HIAA ↓ Carcinoid syndrome ↓ Liver metastases allow mediators into systemic circulation ↓ Primary usually small-bowel neuroendocrine tumour
exam_trap: B, Liver parenchyma — the liver lesions are obvious on imaging, but they are metastases that unmask the syndrome, not the primary source.
takeaway: Carcinoid syndrome usually arises from a small-bowel neuroendocrine tumour with liver metastases.

stem:
During a telephone consultation, a 24-year-old man explains that for a few weeks bread and meat seem to hold up partway down after he swallows, before eventually going through. It does not hurt, he has not vomited blood and his weight is steady.

Which term best describes his symptom?
why_correct: Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing, including the sensation of food holding up on its way down. He specifically reports no pain, which excludes odynophagia. Any new dysphagia needs assessment for its cause.
why_wrong: A. Odynophagia is pain on swallowing, which he denies. B. Dyspepsia describes indigestion-type upper abdominal discomfort. C. Regurgitation is the effortless return of food or acid into the mouth. E. Haematemesis is vomiting blood.
pearl: Dysphagia for solids that progresses to liquids suggests a mechanical obstruction; difficulty with both from the start suggests a motility disorder such as achalasia.
thinking: Food holds up after swallowing ↓ No pain on swallowing ↓ Not vomiting or regurgitating ↓ Difficulty swallowing ↓ Dysphagia
exam_trap: A, Odynophagia — it also relates to swallowing, but means pain on swallowing, which he does not have.
takeaway: Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing; odynophagia is painful swallowing.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after fainting in the bathroom. She has been passing jet-black, sticky, offensive stools since yesterday. Her pulse is fast and she feels light-headed on sitting up.

From which part of the body is the blood loss most likely arising?
why_correct: Melaena results from blood being digested as it passes through the gut, so it usually indicates bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz, from the oesophagus, stomach or duodenum. Collapse, tachycardia and postural dizziness show significant volume loss. She needs resuscitation, risk assessment and endoscopy.
why_wrong: A. Anal canal bleeding produces bright red blood on the paper or in the pan. B. Retroperitoneal bleeding causes pain and shock but no blood in the stool. C. Urinary tract bleeding causes haematuria. D. Sigmoid bleeding, for example from diverticula, usually produces fresh or dark red blood.
pearl: A raised urea out of proportion to creatinine supports an upper GI source, as digested blood protein is absorbed and metabolised.
thinking: Black, tarry, offensive stool ↓ Blood has been digested ↓ Source proximal to ligament of Treitz ↓ Tachycardia and syncope mean significant loss ↓ Upper GI bleed
exam_trap: D, Sigmoid colon — colonic bleeding is common in older adults, but it usually gives red or maroon blood rather than black tarry stool.
takeaway: Melaena with haemodynamic compromise means a significant upper GI bleed until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 58-year-old man is brought by ambulance after vomiting a large quantity of bright red blood at a homeless hostel. He is jaundiced, with spider naevi on his chest, a distended abdomen with shifting dullness and a palpable spleen.

What is the most likely source of the bleeding?
why_correct: Jaundice, spider naevi, ascites and splenomegaly indicate chronic liver disease with portal hypertension. Portal hypertension opens portosystemic collaterals at the gastro-oesophageal junction, and these varices can rupture, causing torrential haematemesis. Variceal bleeding carries a high mortality and needs urgent resuscitation, terlipressin, antibiotics and endoscopy.
why_wrong: B. Diverticular bleeding causes rectal bleeding, not haematemesis. C. Pyloric obstruction causes projectile vomiting of undigested food, not large-volume blood. D. Haemorrhoids bleed per rectum. E. An anal fissure causes painful small-volume rectal bleeding.
pearl: Patients with cirrhosis presenting with upper GI bleeding should receive prophylactic antibiotics, which reduce infection, rebleeding and mortality.
thinking: Large-volume fresh haematemesis ↓ Signs of chronic liver disease ↓ Splenomegaly and ascites suggest portal hypertension ↓ Collaterals form at the lower oesophagus ↓ Ruptured varices
exam_trap: C, Pyloric obstruction — it causes forceful vomiting in the upper gut, but the vomitus is food, not a large volume of fresh blood.
takeaway: Haematemesis with stigmata of chronic liver disease is variceal until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 67-year-old woman on the medical admissions unit has vomited coffee-ground material twice and has had a black stool overnight. She has been resuscitated and is now stable.

Which investigation should be arranged to locate the source and allow treatment?

options.A: Lower bowel examination with a flexible sigmoidoscope
options.D: Ultrasound of the abdomen with Doppler
options.E: Magnetic resonance imaging of the head

why_correct: Coffee-ground vomiting and melaena indicate an upper GI bleed. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy shows the bleeding lesion directly and allows therapy such as clipping, adrenaline injection, thermal coagulation or banding in the same procedure. NICE advises endoscopy immediately after resuscitation for unstable patients and within 24 hours of admission for everyone else.
why_wrong: A. Flexible sigmoidoscopy views only the distal colon. C. Colonoscopy cannot reach a source in the oesophagus, stomach or duodenum. D. Ultrasound cannot see mucosal lesions or stop bleeding. E. Head imaging has no role in finding a GI bleed.
pearl: The Glasgow-Blatchford score is used at first assessment of upper GI bleeding, and the full Rockall score after endoscopy.
thinking: Coffee-ground vomit and melaena ↓ Upper GI bleed ↓ Resuscitate first ↓ Need to identify and treat the lesion ↓ Upper GI endoscopy
exam_trap: C, Full colonoscopy after bowel preparation — it is the standard test for rectal bleeding, but melaena here comes from an upper source beyond its reach.
takeaway: Upper GI endoscopy both diagnoses and treats the source of an upper GI bleed.
notes: Reviewer fix: Made NICE CG141 endoscopy timing precise: immediately after resuscitation if unstable, within 24 hours for others

stem:
A 53-year-old woman with primary biliary cholangitis and portal hypertension is admitted with haematemesis. After resuscitation and drug therapy, an urgent endoscopy shows actively bleeding varices in the lower oesophagus.

Which endoscopic procedure is preferred to control the bleeding?
correct_answer: B. Band ligation of the varices
why_correct: Endoscopic band ligation is the treatment of choice for bleeding oesophageal varices. Elastic bands are placed around the varices, strangulating them so they thrombose and slough. If bleeding continues despite banding, options include balloon tamponade as a bridge and a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS).
why_wrong: A. ERCP sphincterotomy treats bile duct stones, not varices. C. Gastric lavage does not stop variceal bleeding. D. Snare polypectomy removes colonic or gastric polyps. E. Appendicectomy treats appendicitis.
pearl: Gastric varices are often treated with injection of a tissue adhesive such as cyanoacrylate rather than banding.
thinking: Haematemesis in portal hypertension ↓ Endoscopy shows bleeding oesophageal varices ↓ Needs endoscopic haemostasis ↓ Bands strangulate the varices ↓ Band ligation
exam_trap: C, Repeated gastric lavage only — it may clear the view, but it does not stop variceal bleeding.
takeaway: Bleeding oesophageal varices are treated endoscopically with band ligation.

stem:
A 46-year-old man taking long-term aspirin rings NHS 111 because, after feeling nauseated, he brought up a cupful of bright red blood with his vomit. He has no cough or breathing problems and has not noticed any change in his stools or urine.

Which term describes this symptom?
why_correct: Haematemesis is vomiting of blood, either fresh red or altered coffee-ground material, and indicates bleeding from the upper GI tract. Here it follows nausea and comes up with vomit, with no respiratory symptoms, so it is not coughed-up blood. Aspirin is a recognised cause of ulcer-related bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Haemoptysis is coughing up blood from the respiratory tract. C. Haematuria is blood in the urine. D. Melaena is black, tarry stool from digested blood. E. Steatorrhoea is pale, fatty, foul-smelling stool.
pearl: Haemoptysis is usually frothy and bright red and is coughed up, whereas haematemesis is acidic, may contain food and may look like coffee grounds.
thinking: Blood brought up with vomiting ↓ No cough or respiratory symptoms ↓ Not stool or urine ↓ Upper GI origin ↓ Haematemesis
exam_trap: A, Haemoptysis — it also means bringing up blood through the mouth, but it is coughed up from the lungs rather than vomited.
takeaway: Vomited blood is haematemesis; coughed-up blood is haemoptysis.

stem:
A 39-year-old night-shift nurse reports heartburn and a sour taste that mostly wake her in the early hours on days off, when she eats a big dinner late and goes straight to bed. She is otherwise well with no alarm features.

Which advice is most likely to reduce her symptoms?

options.A: Lie flat for an hour after each meal
options.B: Leave a gap of a few hours between her last meal and going to bed
options.C: Have a nightcap of alcohol to help her sleep
options.D: Move more of her daily food into the evening meal
options.E: Have a cigarette after eating to aid digestion

correct_answer: B. Leave a gap of a few hours between her last meal and going to bed
why_correct: Lying down with a full stomach favours reflux of acid into the oesophagus, which explains her nocturnal symptoms. Eating smaller evening meals and allowing a few hours before lying down reduces nocturnal reflux. Raising the head of the bed, weight loss if overweight, and stopping smoking are other recommended measures.
why_wrong: A. Lying flat after eating encourages reflux. C. Alcohol relaxes the lower oesophageal sphincter and worsens symptoms. D. A larger evening meal increases gastric distension and night-time reflux. E. Smoking lowers sphincter tone and worsens reflux.
pearl: Raising the head of the bed is more effective for nocturnal reflux than simply adding pillows, which can bend the abdomen and increase pressure.
thinking: Heartburn waking her at night ↓ Large late meal then lying down ↓ Gravity and gastric distension favour reflux ↓ No alarm features so lifestyle first ↓ Avoid eating close to bedtime
exam_trap: C, Have a nightcap of alcohol to help her sleep — it may seem to help sleep, but alcohol relaxes the lower oesophageal sphincter and worsens reflux.
takeaway: Avoiding large meals shortly before lying down reduces nocturnal reflux.

stem:
A 62-year-old overweight man who has had heartburn for twenty years asks his gastroenterologist why he has been booked for repeat endoscopies every few years.

Which consequence of his acid exposure could eventually turn into a cancer of the lower gullet?
why_correct: Chronic acid exposure can cause the squamous lining of the lower oesophagus to be replaced by columnar epithelium with intestinal metaplasia, known as Barrett's oesophagus. This is a premalignant change that can progress through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma, which is why patients are offered endoscopic surveillance. Risk is higher in older, obese men with long-standing reflux.
why_wrong: B. A peptic stricture causes dysphagia but is not premalignant. C. A hiatus hernia predisposes to reflux rather than being a cancer precursor. D. Candida oesophagitis is an infection, usually in immunosuppressed patients. E. Eosinophilic oesophagitis is an allergic condition, not a reflux complication.
pearl: Squamous cell carcinoma usually affects the upper and middle oesophagus and is linked to smoking and alcohol; adenocarcinoma affects the lower third and is linked to reflux and Barrett's.
thinking: Long-standing reflux ↓ Enrolled in surveillance endoscopy ↓ Need a premalignant reflux complication ↓ Intestinal metaplasia of the lower oesophagus ↓ Barrett's oesophagus
exam_trap: C, Sliding hiatus hernia — it is closely linked to reflux, but it is a cause of reflux, not a premalignant change.
takeaway: Barrett's oesophagus is the premalignant complication of chronic reflux that leads to adenocarcinoma.

stem:
A 64-year-old woman has had indigestion for a year, which she treats with antacids. At a review appointment she mentions that over the last two months meat has started to stick on the way down.

Which of her symptoms is the most important red flag requiring urgent referral?
why_correct: New difficulty swallowing is an alarm feature for oesophageal or gastric cancer at any age. NICE recommends an urgent direct-access upper GI endoscopy for anyone with dysphagia. Her long history of reflux-type symptoms adds to the concern about a stricture or malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Belching is common and non-specific in dyspepsia. C. Flatulence is a benign, non-specific symptom. D. Hunger between meals is not a red flag. E. Occasional hiccups are usually benign.
pearl: Dysphagia is an indication for urgent endoscopy regardless of age, whereas dyspepsia alone needs additional features such as weight loss and older age.
thinking: Long-standing indigestion ↓ New symptom of food sticking ↓ Dysphagia is an alarm feature ↓ Possible stricture or cancer ↓ Urgent endoscopy referral
exam_trap: A, Burping after meals — it is the most frequently reported symptom, but it is benign and non-specific.
takeaway: New dysphagia is a red flag that needs urgent upper GI endoscopy.

presentation: Chronic hepatitis B and hepatocellular carcinoma
stem:
A 44-year-old man who moved to the UK from West Africa is found to be HBsAg positive on blood donation screening, with the antigen still present when retested six months later. He feels well. His GP explains that this infection needs lifelong follow-up because it can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

Which virus is responsible?
why_correct: Persistence of hepatitis B surface antigen for more than six months defines chronic hepatitis B infection. Chronic HBV can cause progressive fibrosis and cirrhosis, and it is also directly oncogenic, so hepatocellular carcinoma can develop even without cirrhosis. This is why people with chronic HBV are kept under specialist follow-up and surveillance.
why_wrong: A. Hepatitis A is spread faecal-orally and causes acute, self-limiting hepatitis without a chronic carrier state. B. Hepatitis E is usually acute and self-limiting; chronic infection occurs mainly in immunosuppressed people and HBsAg is not a marker of it. C. Epstein-Barr virus can cause a mild hepatitis in glandular fever but not a chronic carrier state with HBsAg. E. Cytomegalovirus can cause hepatitis in the immunocompromised but is not linked to HBsAg or liver cancer in this way.
pearl: Hepatitis B can cause hepatocellular carcinoma in a non-cirrhotic liver because viral DNA integrates into the host genome, so surveillance decisions are not based on cirrhosis alone.
thinking: HBsAg positive on screening ↓ Still positive after six months ↓ This defines chronic hepatitis B ↓ Chronic HBV leads to fibrosis, cirrhosis and is oncogenic ↓ Hepatitis B virus is the answer
exam_trap: B, Hepatitis E virus — it is another hepatitis virus that can become chronic in transplant recipients, but HBsAg is specific to hepatitis B and HEV is not a major cause of liver cancer.
takeaway: Hepatitis B can become chronic and raises the long-term risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

stem:
A 57-year-old female teacher sees her GP with several months of a dry cough that is worse at night and on lying flat, a hoarse voice by the end of the day and frequent throat clearing. Her chest examination and chest X-ray are normal and she does not smoke. On direct questioning she admits to a sour taste in her mouth and burning behind the sternum after large meals.

Which condition is most likely to explain her respiratory and laryngeal symptoms?
why_correct: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease can cause extra-oesophageal symptoms such as chronic cough, hoarseness, throat clearing and a sensation of a lump in the throat, through acid irritation of the larynx and reflex vagal mechanisms. Her nocturnal and postural cough together with heartburn and acid brash point to reflux as the unifying cause.
why_wrong: A. Achalasia presents with progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids and regurgitation of undigested food, not heartburn after meals. B. Eosinophilic oesophagitis typically causes dysphagia and food bolus impaction, often in young atopic men. C. Diffuse oesophageal spasm causes episodic chest pain and intermittent dysphagia rather than cough and hoarseness. D. Oesophageal candidiasis causes painful swallowing, usually in immunosuppressed people or inhaled steroid users.
pearl: Reflux is one of the commonest causes of chronic cough in non-smokers with a normal chest X-ray, alongside asthma and upper airway cough syndrome.
thinking: Chronic cough and hoarseness in a non-smoker ↓ Normal chest examination and X-ray ↓ Worse lying flat and at night ↓ Heartburn and acid taste after meals ↓ Extra-oesophageal manifestation of reflux disease
exam_trap: A, Achalasia — it also causes nocturnal cough from regurgitation and aspiration, but the leading symptom would be dysphagia to both solids and liquids, which she does not have.
takeaway: Chronic cough, hoarseness and throat clearing in someone with heartburn should prompt consideration of reflux disease.

stem:
A 26-year-old man attends his GP with iron deficiency and intermittent bloating. He read online that gluten may be the cause and has followed a strict gluten-free diet for the past two months, which has helped. He asks for a blood test to confirm coeliac disease and wants to stay off gluten while the tests are done.

What is the main concern about testing him now?

options.A: The serology will be falsely positive because gluten-free foods contain cross-reacting proteins
options.B: His antibody levels may have fallen, so a negative result could be falsely reassuring
options.C: Genetic HLA testing becomes unreliable after gluten is removed
options.D: A gluten-free diet causes villous atrophy that mimics coeliac disease
options.E: Iron deficiency prevents the laboratory from measuring tTG antibodies

correct_answer: B. His antibody levels may have fallen, so a negative result could be falsely reassuring
why_correct: Coeliac serology and duodenal biopsy depend on an ongoing immune response to gluten. After weeks of strict avoidance, tTG antibody levels fall and the mucosa begins to heal, so a negative result may be falsely reassuring. NICE advises that people should eat some gluten in more than one meal every day for at least six weeks before testing.
why_wrong: A. Gluten-free foods do not cause false-positive coeliac antibodies; the risk is the opposite. C. HLA-DQ2/DQ8 status is genetic and does not change with diet. D. Removing gluten allows the villi to recover; it does not cause atrophy. E. Iron deficiency does not interfere with antibody assays; total IgA, not iron, is checked alongside tTG.
pearl: Always check total IgA with tTG antibodies, because IgA deficiency is more common in coeliac disease and gives a false-negative IgA tTG result.
thinking: Suspected coeliac disease ↓ Already gluten-free for weeks ↓ Antibodies and mucosal changes depend on gluten exposure ↓ Testing now risks a false-negative result ↓ Advise reintroducing gluten before testing
exam_trap: C, Genetic HLA testing becomes unreliable — HLA typing is part of some coeliac work-ups and sounds diet-dependent, but genes do not change; it is the antibody response that falls.
takeaway: Coeliac testing should be done while the patient is eating gluten, otherwise a negative result may be false.

stem:
A 52-year-old man of Irish descent has fatigue, aching in the knuckles of his index and middle fingers, and erectile dysfunction. His skin looks bronzed even in winter. Transferrin saturation and ferritin are both markedly raised and genetic testing confirms homozygosity for the C282Y mutation.

Which organ is the principal site of iron accumulation and of the most serious long-term complications?
why_correct: In hereditary haemochromatosis, excess absorbed iron is deposited mainly in hepatocytes. This causes hepatomegaly, fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis, which in turn carries a high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. The liver is therefore the main organ affected and the main driver of mortality, although the pancreas, heart, joints, skin and pituitary are also involved.
why_wrong: A. The kidneys are not a characteristic site of iron loading in haemochromatosis. B. The lungs are not a typical target organ. D. In hereditary haemochromatosis iron loads parenchymal cells such as hepatocytes; the spleen is relatively spared compared with transfusional overload. E. The thyroid can occasionally be affected but is not the principal organ.
pearl: Venesection is the mainstay of treatment, and if it is started before cirrhosis develops, life expectancy can be normal.
thinking: Fatigue, arthropathy of the second and third MCP joints and bronzed skin ↓ Raised transferrin saturation and ferritin ↓ C282Y homozygote confirms hereditary haemochromatosis ↓ Iron deposits mainly in hepatocytes ↓ Liver fibrosis, cirrhosis and liver cancer
exam_trap: D, Spleen — iron overload from repeated transfusion loads macrophages in the spleen, but in hereditary haemochromatosis it is the parenchymal cells of the liver that bear the brunt.
takeaway: In hereditary haemochromatosis the liver is the main site of iron deposition, leading to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

stem:
An 81-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation and heart failure is on the cardiology ward. Yesterday she became markedly hypotensive after an extra dose of her diuretic and needed fluids. This morning she describes cramping pain in the left side of her abdomen, and a few hours later she passes loose stool mixed with dark red blood. She is tender in the left iliac fossa without peritonism.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A period of low blood pressure in an older patient with vascular disease can reduce flow to watershed areas of the colon such as the splenic flexure. This classically produces crampy left-sided pain followed within hours by bloody diarrhoea, with tenderness but no peritonism. These features fit non-occlusive ischaemic colitis.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids cause painless bright red blood on the paper or in the pan, not cramping abdominal pain. B. Diverticular bleeding is typically sudden, large-volume and painless. C. Ulcerative colitis usually presents in younger adults with a longer history of bloody diarrhoea and urgency, not after a hypotensive episode. D. An anal fissure causes sharp pain on defecation with streaks of fresh blood, not colicky abdominal pain.
pearl: The splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction are watershed zones and are most vulnerable to ischaemia when perfusion falls.
thinking: Older patient with vascular risk factors ↓ Recent hypotensive episode ↓ Crampy left-sided pain then bloody loose stool ↓ Left iliac fossa tenderness ↓ Low-flow ischaemia of the colon
exam_trap: B, Diverticular bleeding — it is the commonest cause of large rectal bleeding in older adults, but it is painless and not preceded by cramping pain after hypotension.
takeaway: Crampy abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhoea after hypotension in an older patient suggests ischaemic colitis.

stem:
A 76-year-old man is brought to the emergency department from his care home with rigors, yellow sclerae and tenderness under the right costal margin. He is tachycardic, his blood pressure is low and his lactate is raised. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct.

Which management plan is most appropriate?

options.A: Immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and fluids, with urgent arrangements for biliary drainage
options.B: IV fluids and analgesia, with antibiotics held until an MRCP has confirmed the cause
options.C: Oral antibiotics and an outpatient MRCP within six weeks
options.D: Emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy as the first step to control the source
options.E: IV antibiotics alone, with elective cholecystectomy in six weeks

correct_answer: A. Immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and fluids, with urgent arrangements for biliary drainage
why_correct: This is acute cholangitis with sepsis: fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain with hypotension and a dilated duct. Sepsis management means giving broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and fluids without delay. Source control in cholangitis is decompression of the obstructed bile duct, usually by ERCP, which should be arranged urgently because antibiotics alone often fail when the duct remains blocked.
why_wrong: B. Antibiotics must not be withheld in sepsis while awaiting imaging. C. Oral treatment and outpatient investigation are unsafe in a septic, hypotensive patient. D. The obstruction is in the common bile duct; emergency cholecystectomy does not drain it and carries high risk in a septic patient. E. Antibiotics without drainage leave an obstructed, infected duct and elective surgery does not address the immediate problem.
pearl: Charcot's triad is fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain; adding hypotension and confusion gives Reynolds' pentad, which signals severe cholangitis.
thinking: Fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain ↓ Hypotension and raised lactate mean sepsis ↓ Dilated common bile duct shows obstruction ↓ Give IV antibiotics and fluids now ↓ Urgent biliary drainage, usually ERCP
exam_trap: D, Emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy — source control sounds right, but the infected bile is trapped in the common bile duct, which needs endoscopic decompression rather than gallbladder removal.
takeaway: Septic cholangitis needs immediate IV antibiotics and resuscitation plus urgent biliary drainage.

stem:
A 64-year-old woman is referred by her GP on a suspected cancer pathway with painless yellowing of her eyes and skin. A CT scan later shows a mass in the head of the pancreas compressing the distal bile duct.

Before the scan, which accompanying features would most strongly have suggested that her jaundice was due to blocked bile flow rather than a pre-hepatic cause?

options.A: Pale stools, dark urine and generalised itch
options.B: Dark stools, normal-coloured urine and no itch
options.C: Black tarry stools and vomiting of blood
options.D: Pallor and splenomegaly with normal-coloured urine
options.E: Bloody diarrhoea with lower abdominal cramps

correct_answer: A. Pale stools, dark urine and generalised itch
why_correct: When bile cannot reach the gut, stercobilin is not formed and stools become pale. Conjugated bilirubin, which is water-soluble, backs up into the blood and is excreted by the kidneys, darkening the urine. Retained bile salts cause generalised itch. This triad points to cholestasis, as seen with a pancreatic head tumour obstructing the duct.
why_wrong: B. Normal or dark stools with normal urine fit unconjugated (pre-hepatic) jaundice, where bile still reaches the gut. C. Melaena and haematemesis indicate upper gastrointestinal bleeding, not cholestasis. D. Pallor, splenomegaly and acholuric jaundice suggest haemolysis. E. Bloody diarrhoea with cramps suggests colitis rather than biliary obstruction.
pearl: Painless obstructive jaundice with a palpable gallbladder suggests malignancy rather than stones (Courvoisier's law).
thinking: Jaundice in an older patient ↓ Pancreatic head mass blocking the bile duct ↓ No bile reaching the gut gives pale stools ↓ Conjugated bilirubin in urine gives dark urine ↓ Bile salts cause itch
exam_trap: D, Pallor and splenomegaly with normal-coloured urine — this describes haemolytic (pre-hepatic) jaundice, where unconjugated bilirubin is not filtered into urine, the opposite of obstruction.
takeaway: Pale stools, dark urine and itch are the hallmarks of obstructive jaundice.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman calls NHS 111 and is advised to see her GP. For a week she has felt exhausted and off her food, with nausea and a dull ache under the right ribs. Her partner has now noticed her eyes are yellow. She takes no regular medicines and drinks little alcohol. Blood tests show ALT and AST raised many times above normal, with only a modest rise in ALP.

Which is the most likely broad diagnosis?
why_correct: A prodrome of malaise, anorexia and nausea followed by jaundice and liver discomfort, with transaminases rising far more than ALP, is a hepatocellular pattern. This describes acute hepatitis, whose causes include viral infection, drugs and toxins, and autoimmune disease, which should then be investigated.
why_wrong: A. Biliary colic causes episodes of severe right upper quadrant pain, usually without jaundice or a marked transaminase rise. B. Haemolysis gives unconjugated jaundice with normal transaminases and no liver tenderness. D. Acute pancreatitis presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and raised lipase or amylase. E. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated jaundice with otherwise normal liver tests.
pearl: In acute hepatitis the transaminases rise far more than ALP; in cholestasis the reverse pattern is seen.
thinking: Prodrome of fatigue, nausea and anorexia ↓ Jaundice with right upper quadrant ache ↓ ALT and AST markedly raised ↓ ALP only modestly raised, so hepatocellular pattern ↓ Acute hepatitis
exam_trap: A, Biliary colic — right upper quadrant pain points towards the gallbladder, but colic is episodic and severe and does not cause a marked rise in transaminases with a viral-type prodrome.
takeaway: Jaundice with a systemic prodrome and markedly raised transaminases indicates acute hepatitis.

stem:
A 23-year-old woman with no history of liver disease is admitted after five days of vomiting and worsening yellowing of her skin. Over the last day her family say she has become muddled and drowsy. Her INR is markedly prolonged and she has a coarse flapping tremor.

What should be suspected?
why_correct: Acute liver failure is the rapid onset of jaundice, coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy in a person without pre-existing chronic liver disease. Her confusion and asterixis show encephalopathy and the prolonged INR shows loss of synthetic function. She needs urgent discussion with a specialist liver unit, and causes such as paracetamol overdose and viral hepatitis should be sought.
why_wrong: A. There is no history of alcohol misuse or chronic liver disease, so decompensated cirrhosis does not fit. B. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated jaundice without coagulopathy or confusion. C. Wernicke encephalopathy causes confusion, ataxia and eye signs, not jaundice and a raised INR. E. Gallstone obstruction causes cholestatic jaundice, but not encephalopathy and coagulopathy in this time frame.
pearl: Paracetamol overdose is the commonest cause of acute liver failure in the UK; the INR (prothrombin time) is a key marker of severity and prognosis and should not be corrected routinely, as it guides transplant decisions.
thinking: Previously healthy liver ↓ Rapid-onset jaundice ↓ Prolonged INR shows synthetic failure ↓ Confusion and asterixis show encephalopathy ↓ Acute liver failure
exam_trap: A, Decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis — jaundice, coagulopathy and encephalopathy also occur here, but by definition acute liver failure arises without pre-existing chronic liver disease, and nothing suggests cirrhosis.
takeaway: Jaundice, coagulopathy and encephalopathy in a previously healthy liver means acute liver failure.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl reworded: INR described as a key marker of severity/prognosis (not 'most sensitive marker') and note not to correct it routinely.

stem:
A 47-year-old woman visits her GP because of persistent itching that has kept her awake for months, and recently her eyes have become slightly yellow. She has no abdominal pain. Liver function tests are requested.

Which result would most strongly indicate a cholestatic rather than a hepatocellular process?

options.A: ALT and AST raised far more than ALP
options.B: ALP raised out of proportion to ALT and AST

correct_answer: B. ALP raised out of proportion to ALT and AST
why_correct: In cholestasis, bile flow is impaired and the biliary epithelium releases alkaline phosphatase, so ALP (with GGT) rises out of proportion to the transaminases. Itch from retained bile salts with jaundice in a middle-aged woman fits a cholestatic process such as primary biliary cholangitis. A raised GGT confirms that the ALP is of liver origin.
why_wrong: A. A predominant transaminase rise indicates hepatocellular injury such as hepatitis. C. Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia suggests haemolysis or Gilbert syndrome. D. Low albumin reflects chronic synthetic dysfunction, malnutrition or protein loss rather than the pattern of injury. E. A prolonged INR reflects synthetic function or vitamin K deficiency, not specifically cholestasis.
pearl: If ALP is raised but GGT is normal, think of a bone source such as Paget disease or bone metastases rather than the liver.
thinking: Pruritus and jaundice ↓ Suggests retained bile salts ↓ Cholestasis raises ALP and GGT ↓ Transaminases only mildly raised ↓ ALP out of proportion to ALT and AST
exam_trap: A, ALT and AST raised far more than ALP — any jaundiced patient may have raised transaminases, but a predominant transaminase rise is the hepatocellular pattern, not cholestasis.
takeaway: A disproportionate rise in ALP (with GGT) relative to the transaminases indicates cholestasis.

stem:
A 66-year-old man is seen in the surgical assessment unit with three days of yellow skin and a vague ache under the right ribs. He is afebrile. An abdominal ultrasound reports a common bile duct that is wider than normal, with dilated ducts inside the liver as well.

What is the most likely mechanism of his jaundice?

options.D: Blockage of the bile duct outside the liver

correct_answer: D. Blockage of the bile duct outside the liver
why_correct: Dilatation of the common bile duct and the intrahepatic ducts on ultrasound shows that bile is backing up behind a blockage in the extrahepatic biliary tree. In this setting the commonest causes are a stone in the common bile duct or a tumour of the pancreatic head or bile duct. MRCP or EUS is then used to identify the cause.
why_wrong: A. Haemolysis causes unconjugated jaundice with normal-calibre bile ducts. B. Viral hepatitis is intrahepatic and does not dilate the bile ducts. C. Reduced bilirubin uptake, as with some drugs, gives unconjugated jaundice with normal ducts. E. Pancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhoea and weight loss, not duct dilatation.
pearl: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging test in jaundice because duct dilatation quickly separates obstructive from non-obstructive causes.
thinking: Jaundice with right upper quadrant ache ↓ Ultrasound shows dilated common bile duct ↓ Intrahepatic ducts also dilated ↓ Bile is backing up behind a blockage ↓ Extrahepatic biliary obstruction
exam_trap: B, Hepatocellular inflammation from viral infection — hepatitis is a common cause of jaundice with right upper quadrant discomfort, but it does not dilate the bile ducts.
takeaway: Jaundice with dilated bile ducts on ultrasound means extrahepatic biliary obstruction.

stem:
A 55-year-old man who has drunk about a bottle of spirits a day for many years is seen in the medical admissions unit with yellow sclerae, spider naevi on his chest and palmar erythema. His GGT is very high and his liver is firm and enlarged.

Which condition best explains these findings?
why_correct: Long-term heavy alcohol use causes a spectrum of alcohol-related liver disease, from fatty liver to alcohol-related hepatitis, fibrosis and cirrhosis. Jaundice with stigmata of chronic liver disease such as spider naevi and palmar erythema, together with a high GGT and hepatomegaly, fits this diagnosis in a heavy drinker.
why_wrong: A. Primary sclerosing cholangitis is associated with ulcerative colitis and causes a cholestatic picture, not linked to alcohol. B. Gilbert syndrome is a benign inherited cause of mild unconjugated jaundice with no liver damage. D. Wilson disease usually presents in children and young adults with liver and neuropsychiatric features. E. Autoimmune hepatitis is more common in women and is not caused by alcohol.
pearl: Abstinence is the single most important intervention in alcohol-related liver disease, and fatty liver can fully reverse if drinking stops.
thinking: Many years of heavy alcohol use ↓ Jaundice ↓ Spider naevi and palmar erythema suggest chronic liver disease ↓ Very high GGT and firm hepatomegaly ↓ Alcohol-related liver disease
exam_trap: D, Wilson disease — it is a classic cause of chronic liver disease, but it presents much younger and there is nothing to link it with heavy drinking.
takeaway: Jaundice and stigmata of chronic liver disease in a long-term heavy drinker point to alcohol-related liver disease.

stem:
A 71-year-old man is investigated for painless jaundice. He has noticed that his urine has become the colour of strong tea and his stools have turned pale. A urine dipstick is positive for bilirubin.

Which form of bilirubin is responsible for this result?
why_correct: In cholestasis, conjugated bilirubin made by the liver cannot drain into the gut and refluxes into the blood. Because it is water-soluble, it is filtered by the kidneys and appears in the urine, giving dark urine and a positive dipstick. Pale stools reflect the lack of bile pigment reaching the bowel.
why_wrong: A. Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and is not water-soluble, so it does not appear in urine. B. Urobilinogen is formed in the gut and falls in complete obstruction because bilirubin does not reach the bowel. D. Stercobilin is a gut pigment that colours stools; its absence explains pale stools. E. Biliverdin is an intermediate in haem breakdown that is rapidly converted to bilirubin and is not what the dipstick detects.
pearl: Bilirubin in the urine always means a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; haemolytic jaundice is described as acholuric for this reason.
thinking: Painless jaundice with dark urine and pale stools ↓ Pattern of obstruction ↓ Conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the gut ↓ It is water-soluble and filtered by the kidney ↓ Conjugated bilirubin causes the positive dipstick
exam_trap: B, Urobilinogen — it is the other bile pigment measured on urine dipstick, but it is produced in the gut and is reduced, not increased, when bile flow is blocked.
takeaway: In cholestatic jaundice, water-soluble conjugated bilirubin spills into the urine and darkens it.

stem:
A 59-year-old man attends the GP surgery after his wife noticed his skin has turned yellow. He says his stools now look putty-coloured and float, and his urine is very dark. Blood tests show a high bilirubin with an ALP several times the upper limit of normal and only a mild rise in ALT.

Which category of jaundice is this?
why_correct: Pale, floating stools and dark urine indicate that conjugated bilirubin is not reaching the gut and is instead being excreted in urine. Combined with an ALP rise far greater than the transaminase rise, this is a cholestatic or obstructive pattern, which in an older man needs urgent imaging to look for a stone or tumour.
why_wrong: A. Haemolysis gives unconjugated jaundice with normal-coloured urine and normal ALP. C. Hepatocellular jaundice shows transaminases raised far more than ALP. D. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated jaundice with otherwise normal liver tests. E. Ineffective erythropoiesis causes unconjugated jaundice with anaemia, not pale stools or a raised ALP.
pearl: New painless jaundice in anyone aged 40 or over should prompt a suspected cancer referral for pancreatic cancer.
thinking: Jaundice in an older man ↓ Pale floating stools and dark urine ↓ Bile is not reaching the gut ↓ ALP raised far more than ALT ↓ Obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice
exam_trap: C, Hepatocellular jaundice from acute hepatitis — hepatitis can also cause dark urine, but the transaminases would dominate rather than the ALP.
takeaway: Pale stools, dark urine and a predominantly raised ALP indicate obstructive jaundice.

stem:
A 35-year-old man with Crohn's disease is seen in the gastroenterology clinic during a flare of diarrhoea and abdominal pain. He also reports that his right ankle and left knee have become warm and swollen over the past fortnight. There is no history of injury and he has no rash or recent sore throat.

What is the most likely cause of his joint symptoms?
why_correct: Peripheral arthritis is the most common extra-intestinal manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease. The type that involves a few large lower-limb joints typically flares with active bowel disease and settles as the bowel inflammation is controlled. Asymmetrical swelling of the knee and ankle during a Crohn's flare fits enteropathic arthritis.
why_wrong: B. Gout typically presents as an acute monoarthritis, often of the first toe joint, and is not linked to bowel flares. C. Osteoarthritis is degenerative and does not cause warm, swollen joints in a young man in step with bowel activity. D. Post-streptococcal arthritis requires a preceding streptococcal throat infection, which he has not had. E. Haemarthrosis follows trauma or occurs with bleeding disorders or anticoagulation.
pearl: Large-joint pauciarticular IBD arthritis follows bowel activity, whereas axial disease such as sacroiliitis runs a course independent of the bowel.
thinking: Known Crohn's disease ↓ Currently flaring ↓ Warm swollen knee and ankle ↓ No trauma, rash or throat infection ↓ Enteropathic arthritis
exam_trap: B, Gout — an acutely warm swollen joint makes crystal arthritis tempting, but two large joints flaring with active Crohn's disease fit an IBD-related arthritis better.
takeaway: Inflammatory arthritis of large lower-limb joints during an IBD flare is enteropathic arthritis.

stem:
A 19-year-old man of East Asian heritage tells his GP that within an hour of drinking a milkshake or eating ice cream he gets gassy bloating, cramping and loose stools. Hard cheese and bread do not cause problems, and he has no weight loss or blood in his stools.

What is the most likely underlying mechanism?

options.A: An IgE-mediated allergy to cow's milk protein
options.B: Reduced brush-border lactase activity in the small intestine
options.C: An immune reaction to gluten damaging the villi

correct_answer: B. Reduced brush-border lactase activity in the small intestine
why_correct: Lactase on the small-bowel brush border splits lactose into glucose and galactose. When lactase activity is low, which is common in people of East Asian and African heritage after childhood, undigested lactose reaches the colon, where it draws in water and is fermented by bacteria, causing bloating, cramps and diarrhoea. Hard cheese contains very little lactose, which is why he tolerates it.
why_wrong: A. IgE-mediated cow's milk allergy causes urticaria, swelling or wheeze, usually in infancy, rather than isolated bloating. C. Coeliac disease is triggered by gluten, yet bread does not upset him. D. Pancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhoea and weight loss with all fatty foods. E. Bile acid malabsorption causes watery diarrhoea, often after ileal disease or cholecystectomy, not specifically after milk.
pearl: Hard cheeses and yoghurt are often tolerated in lactose intolerance because they contain little lactose or contain bacteria that help digest it.
thinking: Symptoms soon after milk-based foods ↓ Bloating, cramps and loose stools ↓ Hard cheese and bread tolerated ↓ No red flags ↓ Low lactase activity
exam_trap: A, An IgE-mediated allergy to cow's milk protein — milk is the trigger, but hard cheese also contains milk protein and allergy causes skin or respiratory reactions, not purely gut fermentation symptoms.
takeaway: Bloating, cramps and diarrhoea after lactose-rich foods reflect lactase deficiency.

stem:
A 46-year-old woman with known gallstones attends the emergency department with severe pain in the upper abdomen that bores through to her back, beginning after a fatty meal. She has vomited several times and is tender in the epigastrium.

Which blood test is most useful to support the suspected diagnosis?
why_correct: The presentation suggests acute pancreatitis, probably gallstone-related. Serum lipase rises when pancreatic enzymes leak from the inflamed gland; it is more specific than amylase and remains raised for longer, so it is the preferred test to support the diagnosis alongside typical pain.
why_wrong: A. Ferritin assesses iron stores and is a non-specific acute phase reactant, not a marker of pancreatitis. B. Troponin is used to look for myocardial injury; it may be checked to exclude a cardiac cause but does not support pancreatitis. C. TSH assesses thyroid function. E. HbA1c reflects average glucose over about three months and is not used in acute pancreatitis.
pearl: Gallstones and alcohol are the two commonest causes of acute pancreatitis in the UK; the height of the enzyme rise does not predict severity.
thinking: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back ↓ Vomiting after a fatty meal ↓ Known gallstones ↓ Suspect acute pancreatitis ↓ Serum lipase supports the diagnosis
exam_trap: B, High-sensitivity troponin — epigastric pain can be cardiac and a troponin may be checked, but it does not help confirm pancreatitis.
takeaway: Serum lipase is the most useful blood test to support a suspected diagnosis of acute pancreatitis.

stem:
A 19-year-old woman is referred to the hepatology clinic with deranged liver enzymes. Her mother has noticed that her handwriting has deteriorated and she has developed a tremor and slurred speech over the last year. Slit-lamp examination shows a golden-brown deposit at the edge of each cornea.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of biliary copper excretion, so copper accumulates in the liver, brain and cornea. A young person with liver disease plus a movement disorder and dysarthria should prompt the diagnosis, and Kayser-Fleischer rings at the corneal limbus are a characteristic sign, particularly with neurological involvement. Low serum caeruloplasmin and raised 24-hour urinary copper support it.
why_wrong: A. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes liver disease and early emphysema, not corneal copper rings or a movement disorder. B. Haemochromatosis is iron overload presenting later in life with liver disease, diabetes, arthropathy and skin pigmentation. C. Primary biliary cholangitis is a cholestatic autoimmune disease of middle-aged women without neurological signs. D. Gilbert syndrome causes harmless intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia only.
pearl: Wilson disease should be considered in anyone under about 40 with unexplained liver disease or a new movement or psychiatric disorder, and it is treatable with copper chelation such as penicillamine or trientine.
thinking: Young adult with abnormal liver tests ↓ New tremor, dysarthria and deteriorating handwriting ↓ Golden-brown corneal limbal ring = Kayser-Fleischer ring ↓ Copper accumulation in liver, brain and eye ↓ Wilson disease
exam_trap: B, Hereditary haemochromatosis — it is the best-known metabolic cause of liver disease from metal overload, but it involves iron, usually presents after middle age and does not cause corneal rings or a movement disorder.
takeaway: Liver disease plus neurological signs in a young person, with Kayser-Fleischer rings, means Wilson disease.

stem:
On a surgical admissions unit, a nurse documents that a 52-year-old woman has just had a large bowel motion consisting mostly of fresh, bright red blood. The team want the correct term for this finding in the notes.

Which term should be used?
why_correct: Haematochezia means the passage of fresh, bright red or maroon blood per rectum. It usually indicates a lower gastrointestinal source, although a brisk upper gastrointestinal bleed can occasionally present this way with haemodynamic instability. Using the correct term helps colleagues triage the likely source quickly.
why_wrong: A. Melaena is black, tarry, offensive stool from digested blood, usually from an upper source. B. Tenesmus is the feeling of incomplete evacuation with straining, not blood loss. C. Haematemesis is vomiting of blood. D. Steatorrhoea is pale, bulky, greasy stool from fat malabsorption.
pearl: Bright red rectal bleeding with shock should prompt consideration of a brisk upper gastrointestinal bleed, so upper endoscopy may be needed even when the blood looks fresh.
thinking: Fresh red blood passed per rectum ↓ Not black or tarry, so not melaena ↓ Not vomited, so not haematemesis ↓ Term for fresh rectal blood ↓ Haematochezia
exam_trap: A, Melaena — both describe blood passed per rectum, but melaena refers specifically to black, tarry stool from digested blood rather than fresh red blood.
takeaway: Haematochezia is fresh red blood per rectum; melaena is black, tarry stool.

stem:
A 45-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis tells his GP that his stools are pale, bulky, greasy and hard to flush. He has lost weight and bruises easily.

Deficiency of which group of nutrients is most expected?

options.C: Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K

correct_answer: C. Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K
why_correct: Pale, greasy, foul stools that are difficult to flush describe steatorrhoea, here from exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Vitamins A, D, E and K are absorbed with dietary fat, so impaired fat digestion leads to their deficiency. Easy bruising fits vitamin K deficiency causing a prolonged prothrombin time.
why_wrong: A. Water-soluble B vitamins are absorbed independently of fat and are not the typical consequence of steatorrhoea. B. B12 absorption can be reduced in pancreatic insufficiency, but it is not the defining deficiency of fat malabsorption and does not explain the bruising. D. Vitamin C is water-soluble and is lost through poor diet, not fat malabsorption. E. Iron and folate are absorbed in the proximal small bowel and are more typical of coeliac disease.
pearl: In exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals is the mainstay, with supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins as needed.
thinking: Chronic pancreatitis ↓ Pale, greasy, hard-to-flush stools = steatorrhoea ↓ Dietary fat not absorbed ↓ Vitamins carried with fat are lost ↓ Deficiency of A, D, E and K (bruising from low K)
exam_trap: E, Iron and folate — these are common malabsorption deficiencies, but they reflect proximal small-bowel mucosal disease such as coeliac disease rather than failure to absorb fat.
takeaway: Steatorrhoea leads to deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

stem:
A 23-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted to a medical ward after several weeks of eating almost nothing. She has lost a great deal of weight and appears cachectic. The dietitian is planning to restart nutrition.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Give her full estimated energy requirements from day one to reverse weight loss quickly
options.B: Keep her nil by mouth for three days to allow the gut to recover
options.C: Introduce feeding gradually with thiamine and close monitoring and replacement of phosphate, potassium and magnesium
options.D: Check electrolytes only after a week of full feeding
options.E: Give subcutaneous insulin with each feed to improve uptake of nutrients

correct_answer: C. Introduce feeding gradually with thiamine and close monitoring and replacement of phosphate, potassium and magnesium
why_correct: She is at high risk of refeeding syndrome, in which carbohydrate intake triggers insulin release and a rapid intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium, with fluid retention and possible cardiac arrhythmias or failure. NICE advises starting at a reduced energy intake and increasing slowly, giving thiamine and vitamin B supplements before and during feeding, and checking and correcting electrolytes from the outset.
why_wrong: A. Full feeding from the start is exactly what precipitates refeeding syndrome in a starved patient. B. Withholding nutrition worsens starvation and has no benefit. D. Electrolytes fall within the first few days, so monitoring must start immediately. E. Insulin is not part of nutritional rehabilitation and would drive phosphate and potassium further into cells.
pearl: Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark biochemical abnormality of refeeding syndrome, typically appearing within the first two to four days of feeding.
thinking: Prolonged near-starvation with severe weight loss ↓ High risk of refeeding syndrome ↓ Feeding drives insulin release and intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium ↓ Start low and increase slowly ↓ Give thiamine and monitor and replace electrolytes
exam_trap: A, Full energy requirements from day one — rapid weight restoration seems like the goal, but in a starved patient it provokes dangerous falls in phosphate, potassium and magnesium.
takeaway: In severe malnutrition, refeed slowly with thiamine and close electrolyte monitoring and replacement.

presentation: Risk stratification in upper GI bleeding
stem:
A 58-year-old man attends the emergency department after two episodes of passing dark, sticky stool overnight. His observations have remained normal since arrival and bloods have been sent, including urea and haemoglobin. The registrar wants to know whether he could be safely managed as an outpatient.

Which scoring system should be used at this first assessment?
why_correct: NICE recommends the Glasgow-Blatchford score for risk assessment at first presentation of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. It uses blood urea, haemoglobin, systolic blood pressure, pulse, melaena, syncope and hepatic or cardiac disease, and identifies very low-risk patients who may be considered for early discharge with outpatient endoscopy.
why_wrong: B. The Wells score estimates the probability of venous thromboembolism. C. The Glasgow Coma Scale measures conscious level, not bleeding risk. D. CURB-65 assesses the severity of community-acquired pneumonia. E. CHA2DS2-VASc estimates stroke risk in atrial fibrillation.
pearl: The full Rockall score includes endoscopic findings and is used after endoscopy, whereas the Glasgow-Blatchford score is used before endoscopy.
thinking: Dark sticky stool suggests upper gastrointestinal bleeding ↓ Stable patient, decision about admission or discharge ↓ Need a pre-endoscopy risk tool ↓ Uses urea, haemoglobin, pulse and blood pressure ↓ Glasgow-Blatchford score
exam_trap: C, Glasgow Coma Scale — the shared 'Glasgow' name tempts, but it measures conscious level and says nothing about bleeding risk.
takeaway: Use the Glasgow-Blatchford score at first assessment of an upper gastrointestinal bleed.

stem:
A 70-year-old woman who takes ferrous sulfate for iron-deficiency anaemia phones NHS 111. For the past day her stools have been jet black, sticky like tar and unusually foul-smelling, and she nearly fainted when she stood up from her chair. Her stools have been dark but formed and odourless since starting iron.

What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Normal dark stools caused by oral iron

why_correct: Oral iron darkens the stool, but it does not make it tarry, sticky and offensive, and it does not cause postural near-syncope. That change in character, together with symptoms of volume loss, indicates melaena from an upper gastrointestinal bleed, and she needs urgent same-day assessment. Her known iron deficiency may itself reflect an occult upper gastrointestinal lesion.
why_wrong: A. Iron makes stools dark grey-green or black but formed and not tarry or foul, and it never causes postural collapse. C. Diverticular bleeding usually presents with red or maroon blood rather than tarry stool. D. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause bleeding or haemodynamic symptoms. E. Haemorrhoids cause bright red blood on the paper or in the pan.
pearl: Melaena usually requires bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz with enough transit time for blood to be digested by gut enzymes and bacteria.
thinking: On oral iron, so dark stools are expected ↓ New change to tarry, sticky, offensive stool ↓ Postural near-syncope suggests significant blood loss ↓ This is melaena, not an iron effect ↓ Upper gastrointestinal bleed needing urgent assessment
exam_trap: A, Normal dark stools caused by oral iron — her iron therapy offers a reassuring explanation, but iron stools are not tarry or offensive and do not cause near-fainting.
takeaway: Tarry, offensive stool with postural symptoms is melaena from an upper gastrointestinal bleed, even in a patient taking iron.

stem:
Over two days, a 63-year-old man on a cardiology ward has passed several loose stools that are jet black, sticky and have a strong, distinctive smell. He now feels light-headed when sitting up. The nursing staff ask which term should be used to describe these stools.

Which term is correct?
why_correct: Melaena is the passage of black, tarry, offensive stool caused by blood that has been altered during transit through the gut. It usually indicates bleeding proximal to the colon, most often from the upper gastrointestinal tract, and his light-headedness suggests the bleed is significant.
why_wrong: A. Haematochezia is fresh red or maroon blood per rectum. B. Steatorrhoea is pale, greasy, bulky stool from fat malabsorption. C. Haematemesis is vomiting of blood. E. Tenesmus is a sensation of incomplete rectal emptying, not a description of stool.
pearl: The characteristic smell of melaena is often noticed before the colour and is a useful bedside clue to upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
thinking: Black, sticky stool ↓ Strong, distinctive odour ↓ Blood digested during gut transit ↓ Light-headedness suggests significant loss ↓ Term is melaena
exam_trap: A, Haematochezia — it also describes blood passed per rectum, but it refers to fresh red blood rather than black, tarry stool.
takeaway: Black, tarry, offensive stool is melaena and usually reflects upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

stem:
A 34-year-old man who had extensive small-bowel resection for Crohn's disease is reviewed in the nutrition clinic. He has lost weight and says he can no longer find his way around his house at night and struggles to see when driving at dusk. His eyes look dry and wrinkled on the conjunctival surface.

Which deficiency is most likely?
why_correct: Vitamin A (retinol) is needed to form rhodopsin in the retinal rods, so deficiency first causes impaired vision in dim light. It also causes conjunctival and corneal dryness (xerophthalmia). As a fat-soluble vitamin, it is lost with fat malabsorption after small-bowel resection.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding and bruising, not night blindness. B. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with gum bleeding and perifollicular haemorrhages. C. Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia, bone pain and proximal weakness. E. B12 deficiency causes anaemia and neuropathy, and optic neuropathy is rare and not selective for dim light.
pearl: Vitamin A deficiency is a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide, and Bitot spots on the conjunctiva are a characteristic sign.
thinking: Malabsorption after small-bowel resection ↓ Fat-soluble vitamins at risk ↓ Poor vision in dim light = night blindness ↓ Dry conjunctiva = xerophthalmia ↓ Vitamin A deficiency
exam_trap: E, Vitamin B12 deficiency — terminal ileal resection does cause B12 deficiency, but it presents with anaemia and neuropathy rather than selective night blindness.
takeaway: Night blindness with dry eyes points to vitamin A deficiency.

stem:
A 49-year-old man with long-standing alcohol dependence is seen by his GP after his partner notices he has become forgetful and irritable. He has had loose stools for weeks, and the skin on his neck, face and the backs of his hands is red, scaly and darkened in a sharply demarcated pattern, worse after time outdoors.

Which deficiency is most likely?
why_correct: Pellagra results from niacin deficiency and classically causes dermatitis in sun-exposed areas, diarrhoea and neuropsychiatric change, the so-called three Ds, and untreated it can be fatal. Alcohol dependence with poor diet is the commonest cause in the UK. The well-demarcated photosensitive rash around the neck is known as Casal necklace.
why_wrong: B. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding, not a photosensitive rash. C. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with gum disease, poor wound healing and perifollicular haemorrhages. D. B12 deficiency can cause cognitive change but not a photosensitive dermatitis or diarrhoea of this type. E. Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain and muscle weakness.
pearl: Pellagra can also occur in carcinoid syndrome, because tryptophan is diverted to serotonin production, and with isoniazid therapy.
thinking: Poor diet with alcohol dependence ↓ Photosensitive, sharply demarcated dermatitis ↓ Chronic diarrhoea ↓ Cognitive and mood change ↓ Dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia = pellagra from niacin deficiency
exam_trap: D, Vitamin B12 deficiency — cognitive change in a malnourished drinker makes B12 tempting, but it does not explain a photosensitive rash with diarrhoea.
takeaway: Dermatitis in sun-exposed skin, diarrhoea and dementia point to niacin deficiency (pellagra).

stem:
A 61-year-old woman who lives alone and drinks heavily is assessed on a medical ward. Over several months she has developed burning feet, numbness in a stocking distribution and weakness climbing stairs. There is mild ankle oedema. She has been eating very little.

Deficiency of which vitamin is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Thiamine deficiency causes beriberi: dry beriberi is a symmetrical sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy with muscle weakness, and wet beriberi adds high-output cardiac failure and oedema. Heavy drinkers with poor intake are at greatest risk. Thiamine should be replaced promptly, and parenterally if Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and dry eyes. B. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with bleeding gums and poor wound healing. C. Vitamin E deficiency can cause neuropathy and ataxia, but it is rare and usually linked to severe fat malabsorption rather than alcohol and poor diet. E. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding.
pearl: In anyone at risk of thiamine deficiency, give thiamine before glucose, because a glucose load can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
thinking: Heavy alcohol use and poor intake ↓ Symmetrical sensory neuropathy with burning feet ↓ Leg muscle weakness ↓ Ankle oedema hints at cardiac involvement ↓ Thiamine deficiency (beriberi)
exam_trap: C, Vitamin E — it can cause a neuropathy, which makes it tempting, but deficiency is rare and seen mainly with fat malabsorption, whereas alcohol and poor diet point to thiamine.
takeaway: Peripheral neuropathy and weakness in a malnourished heavy drinker suggest thiamine deficiency.
notes: Reviewer fix: thinking: 'Proximal weakness' changed to 'Leg muscle weakness' (beriberi weakness is not characteristically proximal)

stem:
A 71-year-old woman in a care home has had sharp pain on swallowing and central chest discomfort for four days. A week ago she was started on weekly alendronic acid and doxycycline for a chest infection. Staff say she takes her tablets with a sip of water at bedtime and lies down straight away. She has no previous indigestion.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Tablets taken with little water before lying down can lodge in the oesophagus and cause a local chemical injury. Doxycycline and bisphosphonates such as alendronic acid are among the commonest culprits, and the typical result is sudden painful swallowing with retrosternal pain. Taking tablets with a full glass of water and staying upright afterwards prevents it.
why_wrong: A. Achalasia causes slowly progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids with regurgitation rather than acute painful swallowing. C. Reflux disease causes heartburn and regurgitation that are usually longer-standing, and she has no history of indigestion. D. Oesophageal candidiasis causes odynophagia mainly in immunosuppressed people or after inhaled or systemic steroids. E. Acute coronary syndrome does not cause pain on swallowing.
pearl: Alendronic acid should be taken on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, and the patient should remain upright for at least 30 minutes afterwards.
thinking: Acute painful swallowing with retrosternal discomfort ↓ Recently started doxycycline and alendronic acid ↓ Tablets taken with little water before lying down ↓ Tablet lodges and injures the mucosa ↓ Pill-induced oesophagitis
exam_trap: C, Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease — lying down after a dose suggests reflux, but the acute painful swallowing straight after starting high-risk tablets points to direct pill injury.
takeaway: Odynophagia after starting doxycycline or a bisphosphonate taken with little water suggests pill-induced oesophagitis.

stem:
A 27-year-old man with ileocolonic Crohn's disease mentions at his gastroenterology review that for two months he has needed to wear a pad because of a small opening beside his anus that keeps leaking pus and occasionally faecal material. He had a perianal abscess drained last year.

Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Crohn's disease causes transmural inflammation, which allows tracts to form between the anal canal or rectum and the perianal skin. A persistently discharging external opening near the anus, especially after a perianal abscess, is typical of a perianal fistula. MRI of the pelvis is used to define the tract before surgical and medical management.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids cause bleeding and prolapsing lumps, not a draining opening. B. Rectal prolapse causes a protruding mass and mucus leakage rather than a discharging skin opening. C. An anal fissure causes sharp pain on defecation and bleeding, not pus discharge from a separate opening. D. A pilonidal sinus lies in the natal cleft over the sacrum, not beside the anus, and does not leak faecal material.
pearl: Perianal abscesses and fistulas can be the first presentation of Crohn's disease, so recurrent or complex perianal sepsis should prompt investigation for it.
thinking: Known Crohn's disease ↓ Transmural inflammation allows abnormal tracts ↓ Previous perianal abscess ↓ Persistent discharge of pus and faecal material from an opening beside the anus ↓ Perianal fistula
exam_trap: D, Pilonidal sinus — it is a discharging sinus in young men, but it lies in the natal cleft and is unrelated to the bowel, so it would not leak faecal material.
takeaway: A persistently discharging perianal opening in Crohn's disease suggests a perianal fistula.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman sees a colorectal surgeon because of anal pain that has not settled with eight weeks of topical treatment. Examination shows two fissures, one on each side of the anal canal rather than in the midline, along with an oedematous skin tag. She also mentions intermittent loose stools and weight loss.

Which underlying condition should be investigated for?
why_correct: Most idiopathic anal fissures lie in the posterior midline, with a minority anteriorly. Fissures that are lateral, multiple, painless or slow to heal are atypical and should prompt a search for secondary causes, of which Crohn's disease is the most important. Her loose stools, weight loss and oedematous tags add to that suspicion.
why_wrong: A. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause mucosal disease such as lateral fissures. B. Constipation causes typical posterior midline fissures, not multiple lateral ones. C. Reflux disease affects the oesophagus and has no link with anal fissures. D. Haemorrhoids cause bleeding and lumps, and do not explain atypical fissures with weight loss.
pearl: Other causes of atypical anal fissures include HIV, syphilis, tuberculosis and anal carcinoma, so examination under anaesthesia and biopsy may be needed.
thinking: Anal fissures not healing with treatment ↓ Located laterally, not in the midline ↓ Multiple, with oedematous skin tags ↓ Loose stools and weight loss ↓ Secondary cause likely: Crohn's disease
exam_trap: B, Simple chronic constipation — it is the commonest cause of fissures, but those are single and in the midline, not multiple and lateral.
takeaway: Multiple, lateral or non-healing anal fissures should prompt investigation for Crohn's disease.

stem:
A 59-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is brought in by his wife because over the past day he has become muddled, sleepy and is reversing his sleep pattern. Examination shows a flapping tremor. He has been well otherwise and has no fever.

Which of the following findings would most likely explain this deterioration?

options.A: Melaena from an upper gastrointestinal bleed

correct_answer: A. Melaena from an upper gastrointestinal bleed
why_correct: Hepatic encephalopathy is often precipitated by an identifiable trigger. Gastrointestinal bleeding delivers a large protein load to the gut, which bacteria break down to ammonia and other nitrogenous compounds that the cirrhotic liver cannot clear. Other common triggers include infection, constipation, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and sedatives.
why_wrong: B. Reducing a diuretic is not a trigger; overdiuresis, dehydration and hypokalaemia are. C. Increased fluid intake does not precipitate encephalopathy. D. Lactulose treats and prevents encephalopathy by reducing ammonia absorption. E. Hepatitis A vaccination is recommended in chronic liver disease and does not cause encephalopathy.
pearl: Constipation is a common and easily reversed trigger, so lactulose titrated to two or three soft stools a day is a mainstay of treatment and prevention.
thinking: Cirrhosis with new confusion, drowsiness and flapping tremor ↓ Hepatic encephalopathy ↓ Look for a precipitant ↓ Blood in the gut provides a protein load converted to ammonia ↓ Upper gastrointestinal bleeding
exam_trap: B, Reduced spironolactone — diuretics are linked with encephalopathy, but it is excessive diuresis with dehydration and hypokalaemia that triggers it, not a dose reduction.
takeaway: Gastrointestinal bleeding is a key precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis.

stem:
A 54-year-old woman with known primary sclerosing cholangitis tells her hepatologist that she has been itching all over, especially at night, and is keeping her husband awake. On examination her skin shows only scratch marks with no wheals, burrows, plaques or vesicles, and nobody else at home is itchy.

What is the most likely cause of her itching?
why_correct: Cholestatic liver disease commonly causes generalised itch that is often worse at night and affects the palms and soles, with no primary skin lesion apart from excoriations. Its mechanism is incompletely understood but involves retained bile acids and other pruritogens. Colestyramine is usually first-line treatment.
why_wrong: A. Urticaria produces transient raised wheals, which are absent. C. Scabies causes burrows, often in the finger webs, and usually affects close contacts. D. Atopic eczema produces dry, inflamed patches in flexures rather than itch with normal skin. E. A drug eruption has a visible rash and there is no new drug here.
