pearl: Itch with no primary rash should always prompt checking liver function, renal function, ferritin, thyroid function and a full blood count for systemic causes.
thinking: Known cholestatic liver disease ↓ Generalised itch, worse at night ↓ Only excoriations, no primary skin lesion ↓ No contacts affected, no new drugs ↓ Cholestasis-related pruritus
exam_trap: C, Scabies infestation — night-time itch is a classic scabies feature, but there are no burrows and no household contacts are affected.
takeaway: Generalised itch without a primary rash in cholestatic liver disease is pruritus due to cholestasis.

stem:
A 69-year-old retired bus driver tells his GP that for the last two months there has been blood mixed in with his stool on most days. He has no anal pain, his bowel habit is otherwise unchanged and his weight is steady. Abdominal and rectal examinations are normal, with no mass felt.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Prescribe a topical haemorrhoid preparation and review if bleeding continues
options.B: Arrange a non-urgent outpatient flexible sigmoidoscopy
options.C: Request an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy first
options.D: Investigate for colorectal cancer using the suspected cancer pathway
options.E: Check haemoglobin and refer only if he becomes anaemic

correct_answer: D. Investigate for colorectal cancer using the suspected cancer pathway
why_correct: Unexplained, persistent rectal bleeding in an older adult must be assumed to be possible colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. NICE suspected cancer guidance, in which faecal immunochemical testing is used to guide referral in primary care, directs these patients towards the urgent suspected cancer pathway rather than empirical treatment or routine follow-up. A normal examination does not exclude cancer.
why_wrong: A. Treating presumed haemorrhoids without investigation risks delaying a cancer diagnosis. B. A routine, non-urgent test is inappropriate when cancer is suspected. C. Fresh blood mixed with stool points to a colorectal source, so upper endoscopy is not the first test. E. Waiting for anaemia to develop delays diagnosis.
pearl: Normal digital rectal examination does not rule out colorectal cancer, as most tumours lie beyond the reach of the examining finger.
thinking: Older adult ↓ Persistent rectal bleeding with no obvious cause ↓ Normal examination does not exclude malignancy ↓ Possible colorectal cancer ↓ Suspected cancer pathway (FIT-guided referral)
exam_trap: A, Topical haemorrhoid preparation — haemorrhoids are common in this age group, but treating empirically without excluding cancer in an older adult can dangerously delay diagnosis.
takeaway: Unexplained persistent rectal bleeding in an older adult needs assessment for colorectal cancer via the suspected cancer pathway.

stem:
Over the past year a 57-year-old woman has bought antacids regularly for heartburn and now books a GP appointment. She lists several things she has noticed recently and wants to know which of them her doctor would be most concerned about.

Which of her symptoms is the most important red flag?

options.A: Burning behind the breastbone after spicy meals
options.C: Sour taste in the mouth when lying flat
options.D: Feeling slightly bloated in the evenings
options.E: Food sticking on the way down, getting steadily worse

correct_answer: E. Food sticking on the way down, getting steadily worse
why_correct: Food sticking that is getting progressively worse is dysphagia, an alarm feature in someone with reflux. It may indicate a peptic stricture, Barrett's-related adenocarcinoma or another oesophageal cancer, so it needs prompt investigation rather than continued self-treatment. NICE advises a suspected cancer pathway referral for anyone presenting with dysphagia.
why_wrong: A. Retrosternal burning after trigger foods is typical uncomplicated reflux. B. Belching is common and non-specific. C. Acid brash on lying flat is a classic reflux symptom, not a red flag. D. Mild evening bloating is non-specific and not an alarm feature.
pearl: Other upper GI alarm features include unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting, haematemesis or melaena, iron-deficiency anaemia and an upper abdominal mass.
thinking: Long-standing reflux being self-treated ↓ Most listed symptoms are typical reflux or non-specific ↓ Progressive food sticking equals dysphagia ↓ Dysphagia suggests stricture or malignancy ↓ Red flag needing urgent assessment
exam_trap: C, Sour taste when lying flat — it sounds like a worsening of disease, but regurgitation is part of ordinary reflux and does not on its own suggest structural or malignant disease.
takeaway: In a patient with reflux, new or progressive dysphagia is a red flag that needs urgent investigation.

stem:
On the hepatology ward, a 61-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and tense ascites has a steadily rising creatinine over a week, with very little urine output. Diuretics were stopped and he was given intravenous albumin, but his kidney function has not improved. Urine dipstick shows no blood or protein, and a renal ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Hepatorenal syndrome is a functional kidney injury in advanced liver disease caused by intense renal vasoconstriction. It is diagnosed when kidney function keeps deteriorating despite stopping diuretics and giving albumin volume expansion, with no shock, nephrotoxins, proteinuria, haematuria or structural abnormality on ultrasound, which matches this picture.
why_wrong: A. Ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis, which excludes obstruction. C. Glomerulonephritis would usually produce blood and protein on dipstick. D. Polycystic kidneys would be enlarged and cystic on ultrasound. E. Pyelonephritis would cause fever, loin pain and an abnormal urine dipstick.
pearl: First-line treatment of hepatorenal syndrome is terlipressin with albumin, but liver transplantation is the only definitive treatment.
thinking: Cirrhosis with ascites and rising creatinine ↓ Oliguria persists after stopping diuretics and giving albumin ↓ Bland urine and normal ultrasound ↓ No structural or intrinsic renal cause ↓ Functional renal failure of liver disease
exam_trap: A, Obstructive uropathy — oliguria with rising creatinine prompts thoughts of obstruction, but the ultrasound has already shown no hydronephrosis.
takeaway: Progressive kidney injury in cirrhosis that fails to respond to albumin, with bland urine and normal kidneys on scan, is hepatorenal syndrome.

stem:
A 45-year-old man whose father died of stomach cancer asks his GP whether any infection could raise his own risk of the same disease.

Which organism is most strongly linked with gastric adenocarcinoma?
why_correct: Chronic Helicobacter pylori infection causes long-term gastritis that can progress through atrophy and intestinal metaplasia to gastric adenocarcinoma. It is the single most important infective risk factor and is classified as a group 1 carcinogen. Eradication in infected people reduces this risk.
why_wrong: B. Epstein-Barr virus is found in a small subset of gastric cancers but is a much less important cause than H. pylori. C. Hepatitis B is linked with hepatocellular carcinoma, not stomach cancer. D. HPV is linked with cervical, anal and oropharyngeal cancers. E. C. difficile causes colitis and has no link with gastric cancer.
pearl: H. pylori is also associated with gastric MALT lymphoma, which can regress after eradication therapy alone.
thinking: Family history of gastric cancer ↓ Question asks about an infective cause ↓ Chronic gastritis drives atrophy and metaplasia ↓ H. pylori is the key organism ↓ Test and treat to reduce risk
exam_trap: B, Epstein-Barr virus — it is a genuine oncogenic virus and appears in some gastric tumours, but its contribution is far smaller than that of H. pylori.
takeaway: Chronic Helicobacter pylori infection is the major infective risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma.
